extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of political theory and public opinion; policymakers and journalists interested in propaganda, mass communication, and democratic governance
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles and evaluative criteria about how public opinion is formed, manipulated, and sustained in modern democracies, with emphasis on leaders' roles, information flows, and the limits of spontaneous popular judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders' informational advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Established leaders are believed to have better sources of information; 'the books and papers are in their offices. They took part in the important conferences. They met the important people. They have responsibility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because leaders have privileged access to facts and contexts, they more easily secure attention and speak convincingly; when evaluating claims, consider the speaker's access to primary information and institutional position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officials as de facto censors/propagandists
rubrics_metrics.description: Every official is 'in some degree a censor' and 'every leader is in some degree a propagandist' because he chooses what facts, in what setting, in what guise he shall permit the public to know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess public communications for selective disclosure and framing; recognize that choices about which facts to release are inherently persuasive acts with institutional incentives (safety vs. candor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture of consent as a technical art
rubrics_metrics.description: The creation of consent has 'improved enormously in technic' and is now 'based on analysis rather than on rule of thumb,' using psychological research coupled with modern means of communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat attempts to shape opinion as systematic practices; examine whether messaging is grounded in empirical audience analysis and modern media techniques, which increase its effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda alters political premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of how to create consent 'will alter every political calculation and modify every political premise' since propaganda makes old constants into variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing political strategy, account for the power of organized persuasion to change assumptions and recalibrate what is considered politically feasible or acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition and casual opinion are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'no longer possible... to believe in the original dogma of democracy; that the knowledge needed for the management of human affairs comes up spontaneously from the human heart.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give priority to measured, recorded, and analyzed information over appeals to intuition, conscience, or casual opinion when forming or evaluating public-policy judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of measurement, record, and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The text stresses the advent of 'measurement and record, quantitative and comparative analysis, the canons of evidence, and the ability of psychological analysis to correct and discount the prejudices of the witness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate public claims by seeking empirical records, quantitative measures, and psychological insights that can validate or correct subjective reports and stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit of self-criticism in the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Without 'an ingrained habit of analyzing opinion when we read, talk, and decide,' realistic opinion will not find support and will be vulnerable to manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote and value critical scrutiny by citizens—encourage routines of checking sources, questioning framing, and detecting 'buncombe'—as a defense against manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical organizers vs. theorists — undervaluation of craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Skilled organizers who 'understood the mystery well enough to create majorities' were often regarded by political science as low fellows, not as possessors of effective knowledge on creating and operating public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing political outcomes, recognize practical techniques of mobilization and persuasion as legitimate and powerful factors, even if disdained by theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited range of individual attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Men can give only 'a little time' to public questions and their attention is confined to matters 'close at hand'; the possibility of spontaneous politics depends on a limited environment of direct and certain knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design public information and engagement efforts cognizant of citizens' limited attention—prioritize clarity, relevance, and local intelligibility when seeking to inform or solicit consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of continuous reporting of the unseen environment
rubrics_metrics.description: The continuous reporting of an unseen environment is feasible and 'often done badly, but the fact that it is done at all shows that it can be done'; engineers, secretaries, intelligence officers, and some journalists provide such reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support and scrutinize institutions that translate distant/complex affairs into usable reports for lay judgment; evaluate the skill and honesty of such reporting as critical to democratic functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotyping and localism in opinion-formation
rubrics_metrics.description: People form pictures of the outside world from 'a few stereotyped images' received from parents, teachers, few newspapers, and rumor; these are little corrected by personal experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of generalized public beliefs that rely on inherited stereotypes; seek empirical correction and broader exposure to counteract parochial misperceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of overgeneralizing citizen competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Democrats assumed the 'omnicompetent citizen' who could manage all public affairs, a doctrine sustained in small communities but problematic when applied universally to complex societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between civic competence appropriate to local, limited domains and the specialized knowledge required for complex modern governance; avoid assuming identical capacity across scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for self-contained communities to preserve democratic spontaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: To preserve spontaneous self-government, democrats sought to 'fence off' ideal communities and confine affairs to the region inhabitants could manage—favoring isolation, self-sufficiency, and limited foreign entanglement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand isolationist or protectionist democratic impulses as responses to informational limits; evaluate policies promoting self-containment in light of their informational and ethical trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security as a precondition for democratic decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy requires 'as little disturbance as possible of the premise of a self-contained community' because insecurity and crises demand quick decisions that masses cannot provide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess democratic resilience by measuring exposure to sudden crises; consider institutional mechanisms that preserve democratic deliberation under stress without shifting power to a few actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion vulnerability to manipulation when based on casual contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Casual opinion, being the product of partial contact, tradition, and personal interests, 'cannot in the nature of things take kindly to a method of political thought based on exact record, measurement, analysis and comparison.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify opinions formed from partial or anecdotal experience as high-risk targets for propaganda; prioritize corrective dissemination of systematic evidence to those opinion domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of reporters and analysts as bridges to unseen facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Engineers, accountants, secretaries, civil servants, intelligence officers, and journalists report distant complexities 'by varying degrees of skill and honesty', bringing them within the range of judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the credibility, competence, and motives of intermediaries who translate complex facts for the public; institutionalize standards for accuracy and transparency in such reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture of consent will be refined and ubiquitous
rubrics_metrics.description: The manufacture of consent 'is capable of great refinements' and 'the opportunities for manipulation open to anyone who understands the process are plain enough.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the ability to shape public opinion as a professional skill with moral and political consequences; implement safeguards (transparency, media literacy, ethical norms) to mitigate abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to convert unseen affairs into accessible, verifiable facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the modern world makes 'distant and complicated events' reportable, the democratic challenge is to present them so 'a really valuable choice could be made by an amateur.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When communicating complex issues to the public, emphasize verifiability, context, and comparability so lay audiences can make informed choices; resist presentations that obscure key evidence.
